final_proof:
Let \(\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}\), and, using the representatives \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\) modulo \(n\), put \(v_k=\zeta^k=e^{2\pi i k/n}\). First, these points are precisely the \(n\)th roots of unity. Indeed, \(v_k^n=e^{2\pi i k}=1\). Conversely, if \(z^n=1\), write \(z=re^{i\theta}\), where \(r\geq 0\). Taking absolute values gives \(r^n=1\), so \(r=1\); moreover, \(e^{in\theta}=1\), and hence \(n\theta=2\pi m\) for some \(m\in\mathbb Z\). Thus \(z=e^{2\pi i m/n}\), which equals \(v_k\) when \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) is the residue of \(m\) modulo \(n\). Also, the \(v_k\) are distinct: if \(v_j=v_k\), then \(e^{2\pi i(j-k)/n}=1\), so \(n\mid(j-k)\); for \(0\leq j,k<n\), this forces \(j=k\). Consequently \(U_n=\{v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}\}\) has exactly \(n\) elements.

For every \(k\), \(|v_k|=1\). Hence all these points lie on the unit circle \(C=\{w\in\mathbb C:|w|=1\}\), whose center is \(0\). Their arguments, in increasing cyclic order, are \(0,2\pi/n,\ldots,2\pi(n-1)/n\). Join each \(v_k\) to \(v_{k+1}\), with subscripts read modulo \(n\), and call the resulting polygon \(P\). This cyclic joining is the boundary of a convex \(n\)-gon. To see this explicitly, rotate any chord \([v_k,v_{k+1}]\) so that the midpoint of its minor arc has argument \(0\). Its endpoints then have arguments \(-\pi/n\) and \(\pi/n\), so the line through them is \(\operatorname{Re} w=\cos(\pi/n)\). Every other \(v_j\) has circular angular distance from \(0\) at least \(\pi/n\), and therefore has real part at most \(\cos(\pi/n)\). Thus each such chord is a supporting edge of the convex hull of the \(v_j\), proving the assertion.

All sides of \(P\) have the same length, since
\[
 |v_{k+1}-v_k|=|\zeta^k(\zeta-1)|=|\zeta-1|=2\sin(\pi/n).
\]
Furthermore, the rotation \(R(w)=\zeta w\) about the origin sends \(v_k\) to \(v_{k+1}\) and sends the two sides incident at \(v_k\) to the two sides incident at \(v_{k+1}\). Rotations preserve angles, so every interior angle of the convex polygon \(P\) is equal to every other one. Hence \(P\) is both equilateral and equiangular, and therefore is a regular \(n\)-sided polygon.

Since every vertex of \(P\) lies on \(C\), the unit circle centered at \(0\), that circle circumscribes \(P\). Finally, \(v_0=e^0=1\), which in Cartesian coordinates is \((1,0)\). This proves both stated properties.
